notes.meaning: God asks Job whether he knows the birthing seasons of wild mountain goats and deer. These shy animals live high up on dangerous rocky crags, completely hidden from human eyes and care. God alone watches over them in their secret places and brings new life safely into the world.

God asks Job if he keeps track of the months these wild animals carry their young or knows the exact day they will give birth. Human shepherds carefully count the days for their domestic herds, but no human attends to these wild beasts. God quietly oversees their entire pregnancy without any help from mankind.

The mother deer crouch down by God-given instinct to give birth safely in the wild. Even without human help during hard labor, they deliver their fawns and end their birth pains. The Lord provides the exact strength and posture they need to bring forth their young.

The young fawns grow strong out in the open wilderness without any grain supplied by farmers. Soon they can care for themselves, so they wander away and no longer need their mothers. God faithfully provides everything these growing creatures need to thrive on their own.

The Lord asks who gave the wild donkey its fierce love of freedom and hatred of human control. While common donkeys carry heavy loads for people, this creature was made to run free. It was God, not man, who gave the wild donkey its untamed nature.

God appointed the barren desert and salty plains to be the home of the wild donkey. Where people would quickly starve or perish, this animal thrives in complete comfort. God provides life and a home even in places that seem harsh and empty to human eyes.

The wild donkey scorns the noise of crowded human cities and refuses to be turned into a work animal. Because he roams free in wide open spaces, no human driver can shout at him or force him to pull a load. He enjoys the untamed liberty that God designed for him.

The wild donkey wanders across rugged hills looking for patches of grass and plants to eat. He prefers searching far and wide for simple food in freedom rather than enjoying rich grain in captivity. God faithfully directs him to find whatever green vegetation is available.

God asks Job whether the massive wild ox would ever willingly become his farm servant. This powerful beast will not stand quietly at a human feeding trough or spend the night tied safely in a barn. Man cannot domesticate what God created to live wild and independent.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars identify this beast as the aurochs, an extinct and massive wild ox that was far larger and fiercer than domestic cattle, rather than a rhinoceros or mythical unicorn.

notes.meaning: Farmers easily strap domestic oxen into a harness, but no human can force a wild ox to dig straight furrows in a field. Nor will this mighty creature follow behind a farmer to break up the soil in the valleys. His immense strength is completely beyond human control.

A tame ox can be trusted with heavy labor because it is gentle and obedient, but the wild ox cannot be trusted at all despite its enormous power. A farmer cannot walk away and leave his hard field work to an uncontrollable beast. God shows that great strength is useless to man without the ability to guide it.

Job could never depend on a wild ox to pull a cart loaded with harvested grain. It will not safely bring home the crops or help gather them onto the threshing floor where seeds are separated from stalks. If Job cannot manage a single wild beast, he cannot direct God's rule over the world.

The ostrich flaps its wings with great pride and joy, but its feathers cannot lift it into the sky like the wings of a stork. Its plumage is beautiful and helps it run like the wind, yet it remains firmly on the ground. God gave different birds different abilities according to His own creative plan.

Unlike other birds that build safe nests high up in trees or rocks, the ostrich lays her eggs right on the open ground. The warmth of the sun and sand helps keep them warm during the heat of the day. God made her to nest in this unusual desert way.

The ostrich leaves her eggs exposed where travelers might step on them or wild animals might trample them. She lacks the natural caution that warns other birds to hide and guard their eggs against sudden danger. Her apparent carelessness illustrates how God created each animal with unique instincts.

The ostrich often seems unconcerned about her eggs and hatchlings, easily walking away if startled by distant noises. Because she lacks the protective affection seen in most mothers, she seems not to worry whether her hard labor of laying eggs succeeds or fails. God highlights this odd trait to show the surprising variety in His creation.

God purposely withheld normal motherly wisdom and sharp understanding from the ostrich. Her silly behavior is not an accident of nature, but something God intentionally designed. Even creatures that appear strange or foolish to humans have their exact place in the Creator's world.

Even though the ostrich cannot fly, God gave her astonishing running speed. When danger approaches, she stands tall, spreads her wings like sails, and easily outruns swift horses and their riders. God gave her special gifts of her own, balancing what she seems to lack.

The Lord turns to the warhorse and asks Job if he gave it such fierce physical strength and courage. Man did not weave the flowing mane that shakes proudly upon the horse's neck like rolling thunder. All of the horse's majesty and power come directly from God.

God asks Job whether he taught the horse to bound forward with the startling power of a leaping locust. The horse's loud, proud snorting from flared nostrils strikes fear into onlookers. God alone placed such fearless vigor into this animal.

Eager for battle, the warhorse paws the ground with his hooves as if digging up the valley floor. He delights in his own great power and charges straight toward the clashing weapons of an opposing army. He shows none of the normal instinct animals have to flee danger.

The warhorse laughs at danger and refuses to panic before overwhelming odds. Even when confronted by drawn swords ready to strike him down, he charges forward without retreating. God gave the warhorse an extraordinary courage that defies self-preservation.

Deadly arrows rattle in the quiver, and bright metal spears and lances flash around the warhorse. These frightening weapons and noises do not cause him to flinch or turn away. He presses straight through the deadly weapons hurled in combat.

Trembling with excitement, the horse races forward so fast he seems to devour the ground beneath his feet. When the war trumpet or ram's horn sounds the call to charge, he is too excited to stand in place. His fierce energy cannot be held back once the battle signal is given.

At the blast of the horn, the horse snorts with eager joy. He senses the approaching battle from far off, picking up the noise and excitement before it arrives. He eagerly listens to the shouting of commanders and the roar of combat.

God asks Job whether human wisdom teaches the hawk how to glide swiftly or when to migrate south for the winter. Birds know exactly when and where to fly by an internal guidance system that no human designed. God alone implants this wonderful instinct into migratory birds.

God asks Job whether the eagle soars into the sky at his command or looks to man for permission to climb high into the air. No human can direct this bird as it climbs toward the clouds or commands where it sets its nest. The eagle obeys God's design alone.

The eagle builds its nest high on sharp, rocky cliffs and dwells there securely. In these inaccessible heights, far above human reach, its home sits safe like a fortified stronghold. God provided this secure fortress for the bird and its young.

From its high perch on the rocks, the eagle scans the plains and valleys far below for food. God gave this bird remarkably sharp vision, allowing it to spot small prey from incredible distances. Man had nothing to do with designing such extraordinary sight.

The eagle feeds its young with fresh prey, and it quickly gathers wherever the slain fall on a battlefield. Even this stark and grim side of nature is part of God's providential care over the earth. God's creation operates according to His own wisdom, entirely outside human control or preferences.
